label: lem:profile
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:profile}
For $1\le i\le m$,
\[
c_i=\min\{i,d+1,m-d,m-i+1\}.
\]
In particular,
\[
c_i=c_{m-i+1}.
\]
head: environment
name: Exact incidence profile

title: Proof
body_md:
The term $K_i$ occurs in the equation indexed by $j$ exactly when
\[
j-d\le i\le j,
\]
with $d+1\le j\le m$. Hence the admissible equation indices are the integers in
\[
[d+1,m]\cap[i,i+d].
\]
Counting this interval gives the displayed minimum. Replacing $i$ by $m-i+1$ leaves the minimum unchanged, proving the mirror symmetry.
head: environment

label: def:mirror
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:mirror}
A base-$B$ Keith number is called a \emph{Keith mirror} if its first return index is even and
\[
C_d(R(N))=R(N).
\]
A Keith mirror of order $d\ge3$ will be called a \emph{higher-order Keith mirror} when the distinction from the exceptional order-$2$ case is useful.
head: environment
name: Keith mirror

title: Remark
body_md: The terminology is structural: Lemma~\ref{lem:profile} shows that the full incidence profile is palindromic. The defining equation $C=R$ then selects the case in which the two central incidences saturate the largest value permitted by the return index. No reversal of the digits of $N$ is involved.
head: environment
name: Why ``mirror''

label: thm:deficit
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:deficit}
For every even index $m=2r>d$,
\[
\Delta_d(m)=
\begin{cases}
2d-m, & m<2d,\\
0, & 2d\le m\le2d+2,\\
m-2d-2, & m>2d+2.
\end{cases}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\boxed{\;\Delta_d(m)=\operatorname{dist}\!\bigl(m,[2d,2d+2]\bigr).\;}
\]
head: environment
name: Exact central deficit law

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{lem:profile} and central symmetry,
\[
C_d(2r)=2\min\{r,d+1,2r-d\}.
\]
If $r<d$, the minimum is $2r-d$, so
\[
\Delta_d(2r)=2r-2(2r-d)=2d-2r=2d-m.
\]
If $d\le r\le d+1$, the minimum is $r$, giving $\Delta_d(2r)=0$. If $r>d+1$, the minimum is $d+1$, so
\[
\Delta_d(2r)=2r-2d-2=m-2d-2.
\]
These are exactly the distances from $m$ to the interval $[2d,2d+2]$.
head: environment

label: cor:saturation
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:saturation}
For even $m>d$,
\[
C_d(m)=m
\]
if and only if
\[
2d\le m\le2d+2.
\]
Hence an even return satisfying incidence saturation must have
\[
\boxed{\;m\in\{2d,2d+2\}.\;}
\]
More generally, if $\Delta_d(m)=2h$, then
\[
m=2d-2h\qquad\text{or}\qquad m=2d+2+2h.
\]
head: environment
name: Two-boundary rigidity

title: Proof
body_md: Immediate from Theorem~\ref{thm:deficit}; because $m$ is even, the zero-defect interval $[2d,2d+2]$ contains only the two integer candidates $2d$ and $2d+2$. The fixed-deficit statement follows by solving the two nonzero branches of the same formula.
head: environment

label: lem:boundary
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:boundary}
For every order $d\ge2$,
\[
K_{2d}=2^{d-1}A-\sum_{k=1}^{d-1}2^{k-1}a_k,
\]
and
\[
K_{2d+2}=(2^{d+1}-1)A-\sum_{k=0}^{d-1}2^{k+1}a_k.
\]
head: environment
name: Boundary coefficients

title: Proof
body_md:
For $1\le j\le d+1$, direct induction from the recurrence gives
\[
K_{d+j}=2^{j-1}A-\sum_{i=1}^{j-1}2^{j-1-i}x_i,
\]
where $x_i=a_{d-i}$. Taking $j=d$ gives the first formula. Taking $j=d+1$ gives
\[
K_{2d+1}=2^dA-\sum_{k=0}^{d-1}2^ka_k.
\]
The sliding-window identity
\[
K_{n+1}=2K_n-K_{n-d}
\]
then yields
\[
K_{2d+2}=2K_{2d+1}-K_{d+1}
=(2^{d+1}-1)A-\sum_{k=0}^{d-1}2^{k+1}a_k,
\]
since $K_{d+1}=A$.
head: environment

label: lem:earlycapacity
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:earlycapacity}
For every $B\ge3$ and $d\ge3$,
\[
f_{d-1}>(B-1)\sum_{\substack{0\le k\le d-2\\f_k<0}}(-f_k).
\]
Consequently,
\[
K_{2d}<N_B
\]
for every $d$-digit seed.
head: environment
name: Early-return capacity

title: Proof
body_md:
For $d=3$ one has
\[
(f_0,f_1,f_2)=(-3,B-3,B^2-2),
\]
so the maximum negative contribution is $3(B-1)$, while
\[
B^2-2>3(B-1)\qquad(B\ge3).
\]

For $d=4$,
\[
(f_0,f_1,f_2,f_3)=(-7,B-7,B^2-6,B^3-4).
\]
For $B\ge7$ the negative capacity is $7(B-1)$, which is smaller than $B^3-4$. For $B=3,4,5,6$, the pairs
\[
(f_3,D)=(23,22),(60,30),(121,36),(212,40)
\]
are obtained directly, where $D$ denotes maximum negative capacity.

For general $d$, ignoring the positive terms can only enlarge the negative capacity, and
\[
\sum_{\substack{0\le k\le d-2\\f_k<0}}(-f_k)
\le 2^{d-2}(2d-3).
\]
If $B\ge4$ and $d\ge5$, it is enough to observe that
\[
B^{d-1}-2^{d-2}>B\,2^{d-2}(2d-3)>(B-1)2^{d-2}(2d-3).
\]
The first inequality follows from
\[
2^{d-2}-\frac14>2d-3,
\]
which holds at $d=5$ and then inductively.

It remains to take $B=3$. For $d=5,6,7$, direct evaluation gives
\[
(f_{d-1},D)=(73,64),(227,162),(697,418).
\]
For $d\ge8$,
\[
D\le2^{d-1}(2d-3).
\]
Set
\[
F_d=3^{d-1}-2^{d-2}-2^{d-1}(2d-3).
\]
Then $F_8=459>0$, and for $d\ge8$,
\[
F_{d+1}-2F_d=3^{d-1}-2^{d+1}>0.
\]
Hence $F_d>0$ for every $d\ge8$, which is exactly
\[
3^{d-1}-2^{d-2}>2^{d-1}(2d-3).
\]
This completes the proof.
head: environment

label: cor:rigidity
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:rigidity}
Every higher-order Keith mirror satisfies
\[
R(N)=2d+2.
\]
head: environment
name: Return rigidity

title: Proof
body_md: Corollary~\ref{cor:saturation} leaves only $2d$ and $2d+2$. Lemma~\ref{lem:earlycapacity} excludes $2d$.
head: environment

label: lem:firstreturn
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:firstreturn}
Let $B\ge3$ and $d\ge3$. If a $d$-digit seed satisfies
\[
K_{2d+2}=N_B,
\]
then $2d+2$ is automatically the first post-seed occurrence of $N_B$.
head: environment
name: Automatic first return

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{lem:earlycapacity}, $K_{2d}<N_B$. We first justify monotonicity on the required interval. Since $K_{d+1}=A$, suppose inductively that $K_n\ge A$ for some $d+1\le n\le2d$. Then $K_{n-d}$ is one of the initial digits and therefore $K_{n-d}\le A$, so the sliding-window identity gives
\[
K_{n+1}-K_n=K_n-K_{n-d}\ge0.
\]
Thus
\[
K_{d+1}\le K_{d+2}\le\cdots\le K_{2d+1}.
\]
In particular, every post-seed term through $K_{2d}$ is at most $K_{2d}<N_B$.

Finally,
\[
K_{2d+2}=K_{2d+1}+K_{2d}+\cdots+K_{d+2}.
\]
All post-seed terms in the displayed sum are positive, so $K_{2d+1}<K_{2d+2}=N_B$. Hence no earlier post-seed term equals $N_B$.
head: environment

label: thm:identity
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:identity}
For $B\ge3$ and $d\ge3$, a $d$-digit seed is a Keith mirror if and only if
\[
\boxed{\;N_B+2Y=(2^{d+1}-1)A\;}.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{d-1}a_ke_k=0,
\]
where
\[
\boxed{\;e_k=B^k+2^{k+1}-(2^{d+1}-1).\;}
\]
head: environment
name: Mirror identity

title: Proof
body_md:
By Corollary~\ref{cor:rigidity}, a mirror must return at $2d+2$. Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary} gives
\[
K_{2d+2}=(2^{d+1}-1)A-2Y.
\]
Thus $K_{2d+2}=N_B$ is precisely the displayed identity. Conversely, the identity gives $K_{2d+2}=N_B$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:firstreturn} makes this the first return. Corollary~\ref{cor:saturation} then gives $C=R$.
head: environment

label: lem:capacity
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Capacity criterion

title: Proof
body_md:
Because $a_{d-1}\ge1$, the positive side of
\[
\sum a_ke_k=0
\]
contains at least $e_{d-1}$. Every negative coefficient can contribute at most $(B-1)(-e_k)$ in absolute value. Therefore the total negative capacity must be at least the leading positive excess.
head: environment

label: prop:B4
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:B4}
If $B\ge4$ and $d\ge7$, then no higher-order Keith mirror exists.
head: environment
name: Exclusion of bases $B\ge4$ at high order

title: Proof
body_md:
For $B=4,d=7$, the coefficients are
\[
(-252,-247,-231,-175,33,833,3969),
\]
so the maximum negative capacity is
\[
3(252+247+231+175)=2715<3969=e_6.
\]

For $B=4,d=8$, the leading excess is
\[
L_{4,8}=4^7-2^8+1=16129,
\]
whereas the crude bound
\[
U_{B,d}=(B-1)(d-1)(2^{d+1}-1)
\]
gives
\[
U_{4,8}=10731.
\]
For fixed $B\ge4$,
\[
L_{B,d+1}>3L_{B,d},
\]
while, for $d\ge8$,
\[
\frac{U_{B,d+1}}{U_{B,d}}
=\frac{d}{d-1}\frac{2^{d+2}-1}{2^{d+1}-1}<3.
\]
Thus the inequality persists for all $d\ge8$.

For $B\ge5,d=7$ the same crude bound already gives
\[
B^6-2^7+1>(B-1)6(2^8-1),
\]
with the smallest case $B=5$ equal to $15498>6120$. The same growth comparison propagates the exclusion to all larger $d$.
head: environment

label: prop:ternary
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:ternary}
For $B=3$, no higher-order Keith mirror exists for $d\ge11$.
head: environment
name: Ternary extinction

title: Proof
body_md:
For $d=11$, the coefficient vector is
\[
(-4092,-4088,-4078,-4052,-3982,-3788,-3238,-1652,2978,16612,57002).
\]
The maximum negative capacity is
\[
2(4092+4088+4078+4052+3982+3788+3238+1652)=57940.
\]
Since $2\cdot57002>57940$, the leading digit must be $1$. Any positive digit at coefficient $16612$ gives total positive excess at least $73614$, and any positive digit at coefficient $2978$ gives at least $59980$; hence those two digits must be zero. The negative side must therefore equal $57002$.

At full negative capacity the value is $57940$, so one would have to remove exactly
\[
57940-57002=938.
\]
But decreasing any negative digit from its maximal value $2$ changes the total by at least $1652$. Hence $938$ is impossible.

For $d=12$, direct capacity gives
\[
e_{11}=3^{11}-2^{12}+1=173052,
\]
while the exact negative capacity is $125712$.

For $d\ge13$, let
\[
L_d=3^{d-1}-2^d+1,
\qquad
U_d=2(d-1)(2^{d+1}-1).
\]
At $d=13$,
\[
L_{13}=523250>393192=U_{13}.
\]
Moreover,
\[
L_{d+1}>\frac52L_d,
\]
because
\[
L_{d+1}-\frac52L_d
=\frac12\,3^{d-1}+\frac12\,2^d-\frac32>0,
\]
whereas
\[
\frac{U_{d+1}}{U_d}
=\frac{d}{d-1}\frac{2^{d+2}-1}{2^{d+1}-1}<\frac52
\]
for $d\ge13$. Thus the capacity inequality fails for every $d\ge13$.
head: environment

label: prop:low-support
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:low-support}
Any higher-order Keith mirror lies in the following finite support:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
 d & \text{possible bases before exact digit solving}\\
\hline
3 & 3\le B\le11\\
4 & 3\le B\le6\\
5,6 & 3\le B\le4\\
7,8,9,10 & B=3\\
\ge11 & \varnothing.
\end{array}
\]
head: environment
name: Low-order support

title: Proof
body_md:
The last two rows are Propositions~\ref{prop:B4} and \ref{prop:ternary}. For $d=3$ the coefficients are
\[
(-12,B-11,B^2-7).
\]
For $B\ge12$, the only negative coefficient is $-12$, and
\[
B^2-7>12(B-1),
\]
so capacity fails.

For $d=4$ the coefficients are
\[
(-28,B-27,B^2-23,B^3-15).
\]
For $B\ge7$, the coefficient $B^2-23$ is positive and the negative capacity is at most
\[
48(B-1),
\]
because $\max\{0,27-B\}\le20$. At $B=7$ one has $B^3-15=328>288=48(B-1)$, and the difference
\[
B^3-15-48(B-1)=B^3-48B+33
\]
is strictly increasing for $B\ge7$. Hence capacity fails for every $B\ge7$.

For $d=5$, the case $B=5$ already has leading excess $594$ and exact negative capacity $576$. For $B\ge6$,
\[
(B-1)(60+58+54)=172(B-1)<B^4-31.
\]
The inequality holds at $B=6$, and $B^4-31-172(B-1)$ is strictly increasing for $B\ge6$.

For $d=6$ and $B\ge5$,
\[
(B-1)(124+122+118)=364(B-1)<B^5-63.
\]
The inequality holds at $B=5$, and $B^5-63-364(B-1)$ is strictly increasing for $B\ge5$.
head: environment

label: thm:support
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:support}
Every higher-order Keith mirror satisfies
\[
d\le10.
\]
Moreover, if $7\le d\le10$, then necessarily
\[
B=3.
\]
head: environment
name: Finite-support theorem

label: cor:35
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:35}
There are exactly
\[
\boxed{35}
\]
Keith mirrors of order $d\ge3$ in bases $B\ge3$.
Their distribution by order is
\[
17,5,2,2,4,0,3,2
\]
for $d=3,4,5,6,7,8,9,10$, respectively.
head: environment
name: Higher-order count

title: Proof
body_md:
Table~\ref{tab:mirrors} contains
\[
17+5+2+2+4+0+3+2=35
\]
solutions. Theorem~\ref{thm:support} excludes every pair outside the finite support, and the exact residual audit excludes every unlisted digit vector inside it.
head: environment

label: prop:d2
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:d2}
Let $B\ge3$ and let $N=(ab)_B$ be a two-digit base-$B$ Keith mirror. Then exactly one of the following holds.

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item $R(N)=4$ and
\[
(a,b)=(1,B-1).
\]
Thus $(1\,(B-1))_B$ is a Keith mirror in every base $B\ge3$.

\item $R(N)=6$ and
\[
a(B-3)=4b.
\]
For $B=3$ this gives $(a,b)=(1,0),(2,0)$. For $B>3$, writing
\[
g=\gcd(B-3,4),
\]
all solutions are
\[
a=\frac{4t}{g},\qquad b=\frac{(B-3)t}{g},
\]
where
\[
1\le t\le
\min\left\{
\left\lfloor\frac{g(B-1)}4\right\rfloor,
\left\lfloor\frac{g(B-1)}{B-3}\right\rfloor
\right\}.
\]
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Complete order-$2$ classification

title: Proof
body_md:
By Corollary~\ref{cor:saturation}, only $m=4$ and $m=6$ are possible. The order-$2$ recurrence gives
\[
K_4=a+2b,
\]
so $aB+b=K_4$ is equivalent to
\[
a(B-1)=b.
\]
The digit bounds force $a=1$ and $b=B-1$.

Likewise
\[
K_6=3a+5b,
\]
so $aB+b=K_6$ is equivalent to
\[
a(B-3)=4b.
\]
The stated parameterization is the standard coprime parameterization after dividing by $g=\gcd(B-3,4)$. The digit bounds give the range of $t$.

In case (i), $K_3=B<N$, so the return at $4$ is first. In case (ii), $K_3<N$; an earlier return at $4$ would require $a(B-1)=b$, incompatible with $a(B-3)=4b$, and $K_5=2a+3b<K_6=N$. Thus the displayed returns are first returns.
head: environment

label: thm:main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main}
For bases $B\ge3$, the Keith mirrors are completely classified as follows.

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*)]
\item Order $d=2$ consists exactly of the two families in Proposition~\ref{prop:d2}.
\item For order $d\ge3$, there are exactly $35$ Keith mirrors, namely the digit strings in Table~\ref{tab:mirrors}.
\item Every higher-order Keith mirror has first return
\[
R=2d+2.
\]
\item No higher-order Keith mirror exists for
\[
d\ge11.
\]
\item If $7\le d\le10$, then every Keith mirror is ternary.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Mirror Theorem

label: prop:triple-extinction
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:triple-extinction}
Let $B\ge3$ and let $N=(x_1\cdots x_d)_B$ be a Keith mirror. If $E_B(N)=R(N)$, then $d\le3$. Consequently every triple alignment satisfies
\[
R=C=E_B\in\{4,6,8\}.
\]
head: environment
name: Triple-alignment extinction

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume first that $d\ge3$. By Corollary~\ref{cor:rigidity},
\[
R=2d+2.
\]
Hence $x_1+x_d=2d+2$. Since both boundary digits are at most $B-1$,
\[
B\ge d+2. \tag{19}
\]
The mirror identity of Theorem~\ref{thm:identity} gives
\[
N_B+2Y=(2^{d+1}-1)A,
\]
with $Y\ge0$. Since $N_B\ge B^{d-1}$ and $A\le d(B-1)<dB$,
\[
B^{d-2}<d\,2^{d+1}. \tag{20}
\]
Combining (19) and (20) would require
\[
(d+2)^{d-2}<d\,2^{d+1}. \tag{21}
\]
At $d=5$ the reverse inequality already holds, because $7^3=343>320=5\cdot2^6$. Moreover, for
\[
Q_d:=\frac{(d+2)^{d-2}}{d2^{d+1}},
\]
one has
\[
\frac{Q_{d+1}}{Q_d}
=\frac{d(d+3)}{2(d+1)}
\left(\frac{d+3}{d+2}\right)^{d-2}>1
\]
for every $d\ge5$. Thus (21) fails for all $d\ge5$.

It remains to exclude $d=4$. Here $R=10$, so $x_1+x_4=10$ and $B\ge6$. The mirror equation becomes
\[
(B^3-15)x_1+(B^2-23)x_2+(B-27)x_3-28x_4=0. \tag{22}
\]
For $10\le B\le26$, using $x_1\ge1$, $x_4\le9$, $x_3\le B-1$, and the positivity of $B^2-23$, the left side is at least
\[
B^3+B^2-28B-240,
\]
which is $580$ at $B=10$ and increases thereafter. For $B\ge27$ every coefficient except the last is nonnegative, and
\[
B^3-15>28(B-1),
\]
so the contribution of $x_1\ge1$ already exceeds the largest possible negative contribution $28x_4\le28(B-1)$. For $B=6,7,8,9$, the endpoint condition forces $x_1\ge11-B$; minimizing the left side of (22) gives respectively
\[
760,\quad1024,\quad1162,\quad1060,
\]
all positive. Hence $d=4$ is impossible.
head: environment

label: cor:triple-eight
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:triple-eight}
Across all bases $B\ge3$, exactly eight Keith mirrors satisfy $R=C=E_B$:
\[
(13)_4,
\]
\[
(42)_5,\quad(33)_7,\quad(24)_{11},\quad(15)_{23},
\]
\[
(444)_5,\quad(236)_7,\quad(197)_{10}.
\]
head: environment
name: Eight cross-base triple alignments

title: Proof
body_md:
For $d=2$, Proposition~\ref{prop:d2} has two branches. On the $R=4$ branch, $(a,b)=(1,B-1)$ and $E_B=a+b=B$, so $E_B=R$ gives $B=4$ and $(13)_4$. On the $R=6$ branch,
\[
a(B-3)=4b,
\]
and $a+b=6$. Hence
\[
a(B+1)=24.
\]
The digit bounds leave exactly $a=1,2,3,4$, producing
\[
(15)_{23},\quad(24)_{11},\quad(33)_7,\quad(42)_5.
\]

For $d=3$, Proposition~\ref{prop:triple-extinction} gives $R=8$. Write $N=(xyz)_B$. Then $x+z=8$ and
\[
K_8=7x+11y+13z.
\]
The return equation $K_8=N_B$ is therefore equivalent to
\[
x(B^2+5)+(B-11)y=96. \tag{23}
\]
The endpoint condition forces $B\ge5$, while (23) is impossible for $B\ge11$. Checking the remaining integer bases $5\le B\le10$ under the digit bounds gives exactly
\[
(444)_5,\qquad(236)_7,\qquad(197)_{10}.
\]
Direct recurrence reconstruction verifies the stated first returns.
head: environment

label: prop:cut-reconstruction
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:cut-reconstruction}
For an even full-window incidence profile with its central cut fixed, either half uniquely determines the other. In particular, if $A$ is known as the complete left half, the unique compatible right half is $\operatorname{rev}(A)$.
head: environment
name: Fixed-cut reconstruction

title: Proof
body_md: The claim is exactly the symmetry $c_i=c_{2r-i+1}$ from Lemma~\ref{lem:profile}, read across the fixed central cut.
head: environment
